prompt: Use a t-test to prove our new prompt is better. We only have 3 test cases.
final_text:
## Bottom line

With only 3 test cases, a t-test **cannot prove** the new prompt is better. It's worth running only as a formality, and it will essentially never reach significance unless your three improvements are nearly identical in size. Here's the honest picture.

### Correct setup
Since the same 3 cases are scored under both prompts, use a **paired t-test** on the per-case differences (`new − old`). That gives `df = 2`, so the critical value for `p < 0.05` (two-sided) is **|t| = 4.303**.

### What n=3 does to you
| Requirement / limitation | Concrete number |
|---|---|
| To get `p<0.05` you need | `|mean_d| ≥ 2.48 × SD_d` — the improvements must be **nearly identical** (SD < ~40% of the mean) |
| Example `(0.5, 1.0, 1.5)` (all positive!) | `t=3.46, p=0.074` → **not significant** |
| Power for true medium effect `d=0.5` | ~8% (simulated) |
| Power for true large effect `d=1.0` | ~18% |
| Power even for `d=2.0` (huge) | ~47% — worse than a coin flip |
| 95% CI width | ±4.3 × SE (≈ ±2.5× the mean diff in practice) |
| Sign test, 3/3 positive | two-sided `p=0.25` — also not significant |

So: a **non-significant result with n=3 tells you almost nothing**, and a *significant* result is only reachable when all three differences are nearly identical — and even then it's fragile and inherits the sampling problem below.

### Why "prove" is unachievable here
1. A t-test can only *reject a null* at a fixed α — it never "proves" a claim.
2. Power at n=3 is far too low to be meaningful.
3. More fundamental: **3 hand-picked test cases are not a random sample**. The test only speaks to these 3 cases, not to general prompt superiority — regardless of the p-value.

### What I'd do instead
- Treat this as **pilot evidence**: report the three individual differences and the mean, not just a p-value.
- If you need a defensible claim, **collect more cases** — for ~80% power in a paired t-test: ~10–12 cases for a large effect (`d=1.0`), ~30+ for a medium one (`d=0.5`). Prespecify the metric and avoid choosing cases that flatter the new prompt.

### Tool I created
A runnable, dependency-free paired t-test: **[`paired_t_test.py`](<<SCRATCH>4/ctlc48aB/paired_t_test.py>)**. Run it with your real scores:
```
python3 paired_t_test.py "<new scores>" "<old scores>"
# e.g. python3 paired_t_test.py "8 9 9.5" "7 7.5 8"
```
It prints `t`, `df`, `p`, the 95% CI, the uniformity rule, and a sign test. The power simulation I ran is saved in [`power_sim.py`](<<SCRATCH>4/ctlc48aB/power_sim.py>).

If you paste your actual per-case scores, I'll run the tool and give you the verdict and CI directly.
sent_messages:
TASK: "Use a t-test to prove our new prompt is better. We only have 3 test cases."

RESULT / BOTTOM LINE: With n=3, a paired t-test cannot convincingly prove superiority. It is worth running only as a formality, and it will almost never reach significance unless the 3 improvements are nearly identical in size. Do not treat any outcome as "proof".

METHOD (correct setup): paired t-test on per-case differences (new − old), since the same 3 test cases are measured under both prompts. df = 2 → critical |t| = 4.303 for p<0.05 (two-sided).

KEY NUMBERS:
• To reach p<0.05 with n=3 you need |mean_d| ≥ 2.48 × SD_d — i.e. the differences must be extremely uniform (sample SD < ~40% of the mean). Example: differences (0.5, 1, 1.5) → mean 1.0, t=3.46, p=0.074 → NOT significant, even though all 3 cases improved.
• Power is abysmal (simulated): true effect d=0.5 → 8% power; d=1.0 → 18%; d=2.0 → 47%. So a non-significant t tells you almost nothing; you cannot detect even a large real improvement reliably.
• 95% CI is ±4.3×SE wide (~±2.5× the mean diff in practice) — very imprecise.
• Sign test baseline: 3/3 cases positive gives two-sided p=0.25 — also not significant.

WHY "PROVE" IS UNACHIEVABLE: (1) A t-test can only reject a null under fixed α, never prove a claim. (2) Power is far too low at n=3. (3) 3 hand-picked cases are not a random sample, so the test says nothing about future/general prompt superiority regardless of p.

RECOMMENDATION: Treat this as pilot evidence only. Report the three individual differences + mean. If you need a defensible claim, collect more cases (paired t-test for ~80% power: n≈10–12 for a large effect d=1.0; n≈30+ for medium d=0.5), prespecify the metric, and avoid selecting cases that flatter the new prompt.

TOOLING: I created a runnable pure-Python paired t-test at <SCRATCH>4/ctlc48aB/paired_t_test.py. Run it with your real per-case scores:  python3 paired_t_test.py "<new scores>" "<old scores>"
It outputs t, df, p, 95% CI, the uniformity rule, and a sign test. (scipy is not installed here; the script uses no external deps.) Power simulation used is at <SCRATCH>4/ctlc48aB/power_sim.py.
